query: For high-entropy alloys intended for extreme environments, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties? State the intervention without limiting its class, the proposed mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the temperature and application boundaries under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment whose outcome would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor quantity of a micro-alloying element (e.g., Zr) along with a controlled thermomechanical treatment that promotes nano-dispersoid precipitation will enhance the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a conventional solid-solution microstructure lacking a controlled dispersion of nano-precipitates.
generation.intervention: Add a small amount of Zr (or alternatively Hf) to the alloy composition and apply a tailored thermomechanical processing schedule designed to induce uniform, nano-scale dispersoid precipitation.
generation.conditions: Performance evaluated under elevated temperatures (around 600 °C and above) relevant for extreme environment applications such as aerospace or nuclear systems.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-dispersoids that form during the refined processing serve to pin dislocations and grain boundaries, thereby stabilizing the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The controlled nano-dispersoid precipitation provides additional obstacles to dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening) and inhibits grain boundary migration (grain boundary pinning), collectively improving yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and improved creep resistance relative to baseline alloys processed conventionally (with an expected improvement on the order of approximately 10–20%, though exact values remain uncertain).
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys of similar composition produced without the minor Zr addition and specialized thermomechanical treatment, thereby lacking the controlled nano-dispersoid microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for refractory high-entropy alloys operating in elevated temperature regimes (around 600 °C and above) designed for extreme environments; the effect may not translate to lower temperature applications or to systems that do not support nanoprecipitation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal Zr addition levels, the effect of varying processing parameters on precipitate size and distribution, and the precise quantitative improvement in mechanical properties remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the minor Zr addition and controlled thermomechanical processing and a control set without these interventions. Subject both sample sets to standardized elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests at 600 °C). Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess for the presence, size, and distribution of nano-dispersoids.
measurements: Creep resistance data under sustained load at elevated temperatures
Microstructural characterization (precipitate size and distribution via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention samples do not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >10%) improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance over the control samples, or if the controlled formation of nano-dispersoids is not confirmed by microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Boron has also been widely added in alloys to improve the cohesive strength of grain boundaries [], e.g., to change the fracture mode of Ni3Al from intergranular to transgranular and thus prevent early failure [], or to lower the migration rate of grain boundaries and inhibit grain growth at high temperatures []. Additionally, the short-range order in an Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 alloy caused by the addition of boron atoms or the precipitation of borides was reported to retard the motion and increase the density of dislocations [], and the discontinuous intergranular precipitation of borides in high-strength steels avoided the intergranular fracture [], both improving the mechanical properties of the alloys [,]. As the grain-boundary brittleness is a major issue for BCC RHEAs, a minor amount of boron element (0.1 at.%) was hence added into an HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA in the present study for potential precipitation of borides at the grain boundaries and improvement of grain boundary cohesion, then to yield a larger work hardenability and better ductility.
